signals.text: This verse (along with the latter half of verse 3) is absent from the earliest Greek papyri (such as the 3rd-century Papyrus 66 and Papyrus 75) and major 4th-century manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus). It is present in the Byzantine majority tradition, as well as early Latin and Syriac translations. It is widely viewed by scholars as an early scribal addition to explain why the disabled gathered at the pool.

topic: Woman accused of adultery; presence and location

local_snapshot.source_text: Καὶ ἐπορεύθη ἕκαστος εἰς τὸν οἶκον αὐτοῦ.
local_snapshot.english_snapshot: And[a] each went to his own home.

signals.text: This verse begins the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11). The entire passage is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts (including 3rd-century papyri and the 4th-century Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) as well as early Coptic and Syriac translations. It is present in the 5th-century Codex Bezae, the Latin tradition, and the later Byzantine majority tradition. In some manuscripts, the story floats to different positions (such as after John 21:25 or Luke 21:38)—clear evidence of an originally independent oral tradition incorporated into the textual stream. It is preserved here due to its theological and pastoral belovedness across 1500 years of Christian reading.

local_snapshot.english_snapshot: And Philip[a] said, “If you believe with all your heart, you may.” And he answered and said, “I believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God.”

signals.text: This verse is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts (including 3rd-century papyri and the 4th-century Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) and early Coptic translations. It is present in the Byzantine majority tradition and the Latin tradition, and was cited by early church fathers like Irenaeus and Cyprian in the late 2nd century. It is often described by scholars as an early baptismal liturgical formula that was later incorporated into the narrative text of Acts.

local_snapshot.english_snapshot: [A] to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus the Messiah, according to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages,

signals.text: Verses 25–27 form a closing doxology that appears in different locations across ancient manuscripts. It is found at the end of chapter 14 in the Byzantine majority tradition, after chapter 15 in the earliest surviving papyrus, and here at the end of chapter 16 in major 4th-century manuscripts and the Latin tradition. Some manuscripts include it in multiple places, while a few omit it entirely. Most modern translations retain it here as the conclusion to Paul's letter.
